content:
Really fun! Great work! :)

The instructions are crystal clear! I’d just clarify to say ‘after 200 turns (100 per player)’ instead of ‘after 200 turns’.

Regarding referee.java, here are a few minor points that I think could pose a risk to the arena:

1. A declared draw is not treated as a draw in the rankings
If the game is stopped after 200 moves, setScore() receives the number of squares each player controls, whilst the viewer and the game description display “Draw”. However, the CG engine classifies the match based on these scores: the match therefore counts as a win.
-> Direct contradiction between the published rule and the recorded result.

Fix: setScore(0) for both players, or rule = “after 200 moves, the player controlling the most squares wins”.

2. No fallback catch block -> referee crash possible
Only TimeoutException, InvalidAction and NumberFormatException are handled.
- player.getOutputs().get(0) throws an IndexOutOfBoundsException if the output is empty.
- Any other RuntimeException is passed up to the engine and causes a ‘referee crash’: no summary, no score, invalid match.
This is the only bug that can cause arena matches to fail after publication.

Fix: catch (Exception e) final -> e.printStackTrace(), deactivate, setScore(-1), addToGameSummary, endGame().

3. Potential risk of the flying orb pool becoming saturated during large cascades
FLYING_POOL_SIZE set to 32. Above this value, animateFlyingOrb returns silently: the missing orbs never appear
Fix (optional): FLYING_POOL_SIZE = 64 or 128 (zero cost, entities created once).

4. The frame budget might be a bit tight
Fix (optional): I’d increase it to setMaxTurns(200 * 45) to be on the safe side (I haven’t actually reached the current limit, but it seems to me that it could be exceeded).

Gratz again!

✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: The game codes are great and work perfectly everything is well organized and I had a smooth experience. Definitely approved!

* Added an explanation on the viewer in the expert rules

* Added a cover picture

Fun game, I have absolutely no idea how I would play (as a human) !

I like a lot the input of the other player's move : that allows to check that your implementation is correct by applying it to your own state representation.

I think it is mostly ready to ship, the only quibble I have is that the explanation of the chain reaction mechanism could be improved. Although the "Game Information" logs gives some hint, I think it would be nice to formalize the notion of "waves". More specifically, I learned the hard way (i.e. not straightforward debugging) that :
- if an orb reaches criticality, it won't explode immediately, but only at the next wave, meaning that if it is hit more during the same wave, it won't be re-gained at size 1
- when the last cell of a player disappears, there will be no more waves : else there could be an infinite loop !

Rules
* Please change "grid" to "board" for consistency with the rest of the statement.

* Please add a comma after "captured by you".

Loss Conditions
* 1st loss condition: Suppose all of Blue's cells have been captured by Red, but some cells on the board are still empty. Blue can still make a legal move and therefore has not lost yet, correct? If so, the first loss condition should be refined. (Both players start the game with no cells, so the condition can technically be true at the beginning of the game even though that's clearly not the intended interpretation.)

* 2nd loss condition: Please change "does not belong to you" to "belongs to the opponent". An empty cell doesn't belong to the player either, yet playing on an empty cell is legal.

Board.java
* Invalid action messages still use integer coordinates instead of chess notation.

Victory Conditions / Referee.java
* The referee code appears to declare a winner when one player owns more cells than the other (`cells0 > cells1` or `cells1 > cells0`). This seems inconsistent with the stated victory condition, which requires owning *all* cells on the board. (It may be that, at the point where these checks are evaluated, the winner always owns all 36 cells and the loser owns none, but I haven't examined the code closely enough to confirm that.)

Thanks.

Protocol change:
* moves use chess notation

Breaking changes:
* smaller board 6x6 for shorter games

Update your bots. Unless someone makes a good case for it, these rule changes are final.

Chain Reaction (aka Critical Mass or Color Wars).
There are many variants of this game and I have still not decided which one to choose:
* placing orbs on neutral cells. Is playing center first an advantage ?
* 4 as a critical mass for all cells. This has the drawback of losing more orbs during explosions and making the game longer (see https://dots-online.com for example)
* smaller board 6x6 for shorter games
* toroïdal board. A bit on the crazy side ...

Hawk eyes ...
All suggested changes implemented

Actually, a "wave" is one step of simultaneous explosions in the chain reaction ( = a frame on CG display).
Regarding the endgame, you nail it. It's a feature: I needed to stop the chain reaction to avoid overflowing the viewer ;-).
Regarding the chain reaction, the exact sequence is:
* you place an orb on a cell. It will explode on the next frame if it becomes critical.
* on explosion, the referee is written so that all critical cells are emptied first and then throw one orb to their neighbours which may eventually become critical and so on.
That means that, if a cell both explodes and gets hit at the same frame, it will end with orbs although it looks to me as an unlikely event.
Good catch. Back to WIP until everything is right.
It should be good now

Yeah, I think I figured it out in the end (maybe not the unlikely edge case you mentioned).

Obviously, I could have read the referee's code instead (I might do that anyway), but I think for the "average" participant, it may be better for the text to be a bit more detailed, possibly in the "expert" section that we often see.

EDIT: Thinking a bit more about it, the edge case is not unlikely, it is impossible : during one wave all exploding cells are of the same "color" (as in black/white of a chessboard), so it is not possible for two neighbors to explode during the same wave.

It's a tiny detail, though, so I'd be perfectly happy for it to be adjusted the next time you update the contribution for something else, or just before changing its status to Ready for Approval.
